title: ‘Killers of the Flower Moon’: Too long for a too short story

commenti.body:
Quite frankly, reviews that focus on runtime are not really worth considering. You’ve said very little about the actual content of the movie and have instead insisted that it could have been shorter without providing any argument as to why. But I guess it’s hard to make an argument about a movie that you fell asleep during.

Side note: you said you fell asleep only an hour into the film which kind of undercuts your point about it being too long and makes it seem like more of a you problem.

It also seems like you missed what makes Ernest a fascinating character. Scorsese has always been fascinated by the evil that men do and why they do it, and Killers of the Flower Moon is no exception. What makes this (and The Irishman) different than something like GoodFellas is that the main characters aren’t charismatic, and the payoff of their evil deeds is a comfortable but unglamorous life. They’re plainly terrible human beings that no one is going to mistakenly idolize like they have Henry Hill or Jordan Belfort.

As opposed to Hale, who is a pure psychopath, Ernest is recognizably human: he’s aghast at the aftermath of the bombing, devastated by the death of his daughter, and even loves Mollie in his own way. However, he repeatedly casts his humanity aside in order to participate in atrocities simply because it will make him richer (being married to Mollie already makes him rich) and because someone told him to, which is what makes him such a pathetic little worm of a human being.

Viewers are often enthralled by the life of crime in the exact same way as the characters are, because it’s glamorous and because the characters are charismatic enough to identify with. By using an unlikable main character who achieves relatively humble gains, the viewer is forced to confront the evil that men do
